title: Cascadable few-photon optical transistor

concept.text: The target innovation is a manufacturable solid-state optical switch in which one or a few control photons determine an optical output strong enough to drive subsequent switches. Cascadability means that these devices can form repeated logic stages: the output of one stage is a usable input to the next, without electrical conversion at every gate. A useful transistor must combine optical gain, compatible inputs and outputs, restoration of degraded signals, and isolation that prevents later stages from disturbing earlier ones.

Conventional optical media have weak nonlinearities, making it difficult for light at single-photon intensities to control another optical signal. Resonators, individual emitters and atomic systems offer routes to stronger interactions, but strong interaction alone does not establish a practical logic device. The defining advance would be to combine few-photon control with reliable circuit operation and reproducible manufacture. The supplied evidence documents relevant progress without establishing whether this complete target remains unmet across the field on 1 November 2026.

significance.text: Electronic transistors made reliable, repeated switching a foundation of information processing. A successful optical counterpart would provide a basis for regenerative optical logic: each stage could make a logic decision and restore a signal sufficiently to continue through a circuit. Direct conditional applications include optical regeneration and processing of communication signals without converting them to electricity at every gate. This is the useful transistor analogy; a single impressive modulation experiment does not yet demonstrate the equivalent of an electronic logic family.

Its advantage for mainstream classical computing would depend on total operating energy and system performance. In January 2010, David Miller described then-current CMOS logic energies at the femtojoule level and projected future targets of tens of attojoules. Those figures are historical benchmarks, not a verified comparison with contemporary CMOS. Few-photon control energy alone cannot establish energy competitiveness: the full operating energy must be counted. Even meeting an energy benchmark would not by itself establish that an optical technology could replace CMOS.

Communication may offer advantages distinct from logic performance, but this transistor alone would establish neither a thousandfold reduction in energy per operation nor elimination of interconnect bottlenecks. Similarly, deterministic coherent photonic quantum logic is a further possibility requiring additional capabilities. An incoherent switch may assist control within quantum hardware, but it does not automatically implement a coherent photon–photon gate. The silicon avalanche approach discussed in the supplied interview does not preserve coherence between the interacting beams.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central engineering challenge is to achieve strong few-photon control while satisfying the requirements of successive logic stages together. The output must drive at least two subsequent inputs, degraded logic levels and beam or pulse quality must be restored, and signals must remain usable despite unequal path losses. Input–output isolation and operation without critical bias adjustment are also necessary within this proposed circuit scope. Improving optical nonlinearity addresses only part of that combined problem.

For the demonstrated silicon avalanche route, the remaining development includes device geometry, diode design, optical coupling, electrical operation and materials. The reported experiment used a commercial single-photon avalanche detector rather than a device optimized as an optical transistor. Proposed integrated-cavity improvements in the supplementary material are development directions, not demonstrated integrated switching performance. Turning the modulation mechanism into a manufacturable circuit therefore requires evidence beyond the reported material response.

For direct deterministic quantum logic, the additional breakthrough would be a suitable coherent photon–photon operation with controlled errors and losses. Classical gain and signal restoration do not establish that capability. Coherence and reversibility introduce separate engineering difficulties, so the classical optical transistor and coherent quantum gate should remain distinct milestones.

current_state.text: Miller’s January 2010 commentary judged that most optical-logic proposals failed several practical circuit requirements. It also acknowledged an earlier device that apparently satisfied the qualitative criteria sufficiently for large logic systems to be constructed. This historical qualification matters: the challenge cannot be described as the complete absence of previous cascadable optical logic. The narrower target here combines solid-state manufacture, few-photon control and the proposed practical operating requirements.

On 17 November 2025, Sychev, Chen and colleagues published a demonstration of all-optical refractive-index modulation in silicon enabled by electron avalanche, using a control beam at single-photon light intensities. The abstract reports an effective nonlinear index n₂ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻² m² W⁻¹. The paper was assigned to Nature Nanotechnology 21, 71–77, in the 2026 issue. The reported coefficient characterizes the demonstrated effective response; it does not by itself establish logic gain, fan-out, restoration, or a repeated circuit.

In an 11 December 2025 interview, the group explicitly described room-temperature operation and characterized the experiment as a proof of principle using an unoptimized commercial single-photon detector. The supplementary text confirms use of a commercial SPAD and describes a pump–probe apparatus. Practical switching still required development of geometry, diode design, coupling, electrical operation and materials. These results establish a promising modulation mechanism, while the supplied evidence does not demonstrate a cascadable logic family based on it.

The research notes also attribute transistor gain of 151 for photons in orbital-angular-momentum modes to a Rydberg-atom experiment by Liao and colleagues, cited as Physical Review Letters 135, 260803, dated 22 December 2025. No retained text for that citation was available to the supplied review. The numerical gain, mode encoding, atomic-ensemble implementation and circuit performance therefore remain unverified within this record. This evidence gap does not show that the reported result is false, and the numerical claim should not be treated as established here.

The supplied review had partial access to the silicon main article through its subscription preview and abstract, together with the complete supplementary document and a full interview. The supplementary document was not the main paper, and its figures were not inspected. No retained Europe PMC text was available, although the silicon result had independent support from the other supplied material. The evidence establishes the dated achievements above but does not provide comprehensive coverage of the field through 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: A convincing circuit demonstration should combine compatible optical inputs and outputs, a complete logic function such as NAND or NOR, fan-out of at least two, restoration of logic levels and beam or pulse quality, input–output isolation, operation without critical biasing, and logic encoding that tolerates unequal path loss. These requirements follow Miller’s practical-logic framework; satisfying only one or two would not establish the combined capability.
completion_criteria.label: Optical logic jointly satisfies practical-logic requirements with fan-out at least two

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: construct a solid-state circuit with at least several repeated stages operating at room temperature, with one or a few photons controlling each switching event. Measure the photon-number distribution and define the control window, switching success probability, logic error rate, operating speed, fan-out and tolerable loss range. Compare total energy per operation with a contemporary CMOS implementation performing a comparable function at stated speed and error requirements. These are proposed acceptance conditions for this innovation’s classical-computing scope, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Several repeated solid-state stages switch using few photons at room temperature

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility boundary: repeat the circuit behavior across multiple fabricated devices and runs, reporting manufacturing variation, allowable bias and temperature ranges, and performance as stage count and path loss change. Energy accounting should explicitly include the resources needed to operate the switch, rather than only the few-photon input. Independent reproduction would strengthen the claim. Finite demonstrations would establish operation across the tested conditions and circuit sizes, without proving unrestricted scalability or literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Circuit reproducibility across fabricated devices includes operating limits and full resource costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed additional quantum milestone: demonstrate a coherent photon–photon gate and characterize its fidelity, loss and preservation of coherence, separately from the classical circuit demonstration. A successful incoherent optical transistor would remain a substantive achievement even if this further quantum capability were not obtained.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Photon–photon gate demonstrates quantified fidelity, loss and coherence preservation

related_concepts.text: OPT-09, “Few-femtojoule optical links inside computing packages,” concerns moving information between components, whereas OPT-01 concerns switching and restoring information through optical logic stages. They may complement one another, but success in either does not establish the other. Miller’s distinction between communication advantages and logic performance supports keeping these capabilities separate.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-02, “Arrays of deterministic single-photon sources above the loss threshold,” concerns supplying photons reliably; OPT-01 concerns using a small optical input to control another optical signal. OPT-03, “Room-temperature, electrically pumped laser grown in a silicon CMOS flow,” concerns an integrated light source and manufacturing compatibility. Both could supply components for future optical circuits, but neither title establishes cascadable few-photon switching.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-10, “Room-temperature short-wave-infrared photon-counting cameras,” concerns photon detection and imaging. Although the silicon experiment used a single-photon detector as its experimental platform, detecting photons and producing compatible optical outputs for successive logic stages are distinct capabilities. OPT-08, “The quantum vacuum as a laboratory nonlinear optical medium,” shares the broad theme of optical interactions, but its stated medium and laboratory objective differ from the manufacturable solid-state transistor targeted here.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-04, “Laboratory-scale coherent hard X-ray source,” OPT-05, “Video-rate cellular imaging through living tissue,” OPT-06, “Practical visible far-field super-resolution optic,” and OPT-07, “Macroscopic programmable visible optical aperture,” address source generation, imaging, resolution and aperture control respectively. Their supplied titles do not establish direct overlap with few-photon regenerative logic. These comparisons are limited to the roster titles, because detailed records for those concepts were not supplied. The research’s suggested equivalence to historical item 4 cannot be assessed without that item.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not determine whether the complete solid-state few-photon cascading target remains unmet across the field on 1 November 2026.
The cited Rydberg experiment’s gain of 151, orbital-angular-momentum operation, implementation and circuit capabilities require source-text verification.

The silicon evidence does not establish complete transistor performance, repeated-stage operation or independent reproducibility; the full main paper and uninspected figures could contain relevant additional detail.
A contemporary CMOS comparison requires a matched function, speed, error target and explicit total-energy accounting.
Operational definitions and acceptance ranges for few-photon control, logic errors, loss tolerance, fabrication variation and scalability remain to be chosen for the proposed demonstration.
The proposed connection to historical item 4 cannot be verified because that entry was not supplied.
Related-concept comparisons beyond OPT-01 are limited to supplied titles rather than full technical records.

brief.title: Light switches that can drive other light switches
possible: Communication equipment could process light signals through chains of switches without turning them into electricity at every step. Each switch would use one or a few photons—packets of light—to control an output strong enough to operate subsequent switches.
why: Each stage could make a logic decision and clean up a weakened or distorted signal before passing it on. That would give designers a basis for building reliable information-processing circuits that work with light.

sources.showed: Miller set out the requirements for practical optical logic. He noted that an earlier device apparently met them well enough to support large logic systems.
sources.cited_for: Practical optical logic requires compatible stages, signal restoration, isolation and enough output to drive subsequent switches.
sources.not_established: The commentary does not demonstrate a manufacturable solid-state circuit controlled by a few photons.

sources.showed: A later version of the same work.

sources.who: Demid V. Sychev, Peigang Chen and colleagues
sources.showed: The team used a control beam at single-photon intensities to change how silicon affects light. An electron avalanche—a chain reaction that frees more electrons—amplified the response.
sources.quote: Here we demonstrate all-optical modulation of the refractive index enabled by the electron avalanche process in silicon using a control beam with single-photon light intensities.
sources.cited_for: Silicon can respond optically to a control beam at single-photon intensities.
sources.not_established: The result does not establish signal restoration or an output that reliably drives repeated switching stages.

sources.who: Demid Sychev and colleagues at Purdue University
sources.showed: The researchers described room-temperature operation using a commercial single-photon detector. They demonstrated a change in a second beam's reflected intensity.
sources.quote: This behavior effectively mimics a photonic transistor, where a single-photon-level signal modulates a macroscopic optical beam,
sources.cited_for: The silicon experiment worked at room temperature but used a detector that was not optimized as an optical switch.
sources.not_established: A practical switch still needs device development, and the method does not preserve coherence, the phase relationships between light waves.

sources.showed: This is an atom-based optical transistor experiment.
sources.cited_for: The experiment concerns another route to controlling light with light.
sources.not_established: An atom-based transistor experiment does not establish a manufacturable solid-state circuit with repeated switching stages.

shown: Sychev, Chen and colleagues demonstrated room-temperature control of silicon's optical response using light at single-photon intensities. Their proof of principle used an unoptimized commercial detector; it did not demonstrate a chain of working optical logic stages.
missing: A circuit must combine few-photon control, signal cleanup, isolation and enough output to drive at least two subsequent switches.
Several solid-state stages must work together at room temperature, with measured errors, speed and tolerance to light loss.
Fabricated devices must repeat the circuit behavior, with manufacturing variation and all operating energy counted.
A separate quantum operation must preserve coherence while controlling errors and photon loss.

milestones.label: Optical logic reliably drives at least two subsequent switches
milestones.explanation: A complete logic circuit must combine compatible stages, signal and pulse cleanup, isolation, tolerance to unequal losses and operation without precise adjustment. These properties let signals survive repeated switching.

milestones.label: Repeated solid-state stages work with few photons at room temperature
milestones.explanation: Several stages must switch at room temperature with measured photon counts, errors, speed and loss tolerance, plus a matched comparison of total energy with electronic logic. This would test useful circuit operation.

milestones.label: Fabricated circuits reproduce performance with full operating costs
milestones.explanation: Multiple fabricated devices and runs must repeat the behavior, with operating limits, variation, stage-count effects and full resource costs measured. This would establish reproducibility within tested conditions.

milestones.label: A quantum light gate preserves coherence with measured errors
milestones.explanation: A separate photon–photon gate, an operation between light packets, must demonstrate accuracy, loss and preservation of coherence. This would establish the additional quantum capability beyond classical switching.

uncertain: Whether any approach already combines the full set of solid-state, few-photon circuit capabilities remains unresolved.
Acceptable photon counts, error rates, losses and manufacturing variation still need defined limits.
Any energy advantage over electronic logic depends on matching the function, speed and error requirements while counting all operating energy.

page.title: Cascadable solid-state single-photon optical transistors
page.definition: A solid-state switch in which one gate photon—a quantum of the control light—controls a larger optical signal. Its output directly drives further logic gates, which restore degraded signals and can each drive at least two subsequent gates; connecting gates in succession is cascading.

goal.need: POLLOC's final report identifies processor clocks of a few gigahertz as a constraint. Its programme objective specifies cascadable optical gates switching below 100 attojoules and in less than one picosecond. Single-photon control addresses optical input energy, but an energy advantage requires counting the total energy per logic operation.

statements.body: European Commission Horizon 2020 POLLOC project, coordinated by IBM Research
statements.quote: we aim for optically programmable, cascadable logic gates with less than 100 attojoule switching energy and sub-picosecond switching speed.
statements.context: The CORDIS fact sheet, updated on 1 September 2025, states the objective of the project that ran from 1 October 2020 to 30 September 2023.

statements.quote: Now our goal is to make a device which will be optimized to work as a single-photon switch.
statements.context: Demid Sychev describes development following the group's silicon electron-avalanche modulation experiment.

completion.title: Single-photon solid-state optical logic restores signals and drives at least two subsequent gates.
completion.criterion: A solid-state optical circuit uses single-photon gate inputs and demonstrates NAND or NOR logic together with compatible input/output wavelengths and beam/pulse shapes, output sufficient to drive at least two subsequent gates, restoration of logic levels and beam/pulse quality, input/output isolation, operation without critical bias adjustment, and logic encoding that tolerates unequal path losses. Optical signals connect the gates without conversion to electrical signals between stages.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas, synthesis of published single-photon switching and optical-logic circuit criteria.
completion.basis: Searches for standards, programme targets and roadmap acceptance criteria, including POLLOC, the 2019 all-optical-processing roadmap and Miller's framework, found no external test combining these requirements. This synthesis joins the published single-photon control test to Miller's six circuit criteria. The cited results establish separate parts of this conjunction.

milestones.title: One gate photon changes the optical output of a solid-state device.
milestones.criterion: One gate photon changes an optical output; conditioned events and weak-pulse averages remain distinct evidence. On 6 July 2018, Sun et al. reported a cavity-coupled quantum-dot spin at 3.6 K, using 63 ps gate pulses with mean 0.21 coupled photons and gate-photon coincidence conditioning. On 22 September 2021, Zasedatelev et al. reported single-photon-level polariton nonlinearity. On 17 November 2025, Sychev et al. reported silicon avalanche modulation at single-photon intensities; their preprint required averaging and could not resolve single-shot events.
milestones.set_by: Single-photon switching convention, operationalized by Sun et al. in their quantum-dot experiment and accompanying manuscript.
milestones.threshold_quote: a single gate photon controls the transmittance

milestones.title: One gate photon changes a solid-state transistor's mean optical output by more than one photon.
milestones.criterion: The gain G, defined as the change in mean transmitted signal-photon number per gate photon, exceeds 1. Sun et al.'s 2018 quantum-dot manuscript reports G = 3.3 ± 0.4 at 29.2 ± 3.2 signal photons, measured by preparing the two spin states; collection losses limit usable gain. The Rydberg-ensemble transistor published on 22 December 2025 reports gain 151, outside the solid-state cases. The silicon modulation coefficient and polariton nonlinearity alone do not establish this photon-count gain.
milestones.set_by: Single-photon-transistor gain convention, explicitly defined and applied by Sun et al.; their numerical experiment concerns a quantum-dot cavity.
milestones.threshold_quote: An important feature of transistors is that they exhibit a gain above unity.

milestones.title: The optical output of one solid-state gate controls a second gate.
milestones.criterion: The first gate's optical output controls a second gate with compatible wavelength, spatial mode and pulse shape. On 25 June 2024, Sannikov et al. reported two cascaded organic-polariton NOT gates, using approximately 4 pJ for the interstage control beam. On 12 January 2026, Tassan et al. reported two coupled polymer-filled resonators with amplification up to 60 and extinction ratio up to 8:1 at femtojoule input energies. The cited silicon avalanche and quantum-dot studies do not demonstrate cascading.
milestones.set_by: Optical-logic cascadability convention, stated and tested by Sannikov et al. in Nature Communications; their experiment used organic polariton gates.
milestones.threshold_quote: the output of one gate to act as an input to another gate

milestones.title: A solid-state NAND or NOR gate restores signals and drives at least two subsequent gates.
milestones.criterion: A solid-state NAND or NOR gate jointly provides compatible optical inputs and outputs, fan-out of at least 2, restoration of logic levels and beam/pulse quality, and input/output isolation. This milestone imposes no single-photon input condition. A 2012 silicon-microring experiment showed approximately 2 dB gate variation producing approximately 18 dB output contrast, a restoration result. That component result and the cited quantum-dot and polariton demonstrations do not establish the combined gate test.
milestones.set_by: Miller's published optical-logic criteria, Box 1 of Nature Photonics, applied subsequently by Varghese et al. to silicon optical transistors.
milestones.threshold_quote: fan-out or signal gain of at least two

not_found: No external acceptance test was found that combines single-photon control with all six circuit criteria in a solid-state optical logic family.
No external numerical acceptance thresholds were found for the combined capability's error probability, fabrication yield or circuit stage count.
The full silicon journal article and its final supplementary PDF were unavailable; its publisher abstract and preprint were readable.
The full 2021 polariton journal article and its supplementary PDF were unavailable; its publisher abstract was readable.
